title: International Money Transfers and Remittances
subtitle: Paying out and sending cross-border transfers correctly, serving diaspora families and spotting AML/CFT and fraud red flags
summary: A practical course for remittance desk and branch staff on how money reaches Ethiopia through money transfer operators, banks and wallets, how to pay out and send transfers under the post-2024 FX rules, and how to protect customers and the bank from fraud and money laundering.
audience: Remittance desk officers, tellers, customer service and branch staff, and international banking staff who pay out or send cross-border transfers. No prerequisites.
objectives: Explain how remittances reach Ethiopia through money transfer operators, banks, wallets and informal channels, and why the formal share grew after July 2024
Pay out inward transfers correctly, with the right identification, conversion, payout channel and records
Process outward transfers within the eligibility rules of FXD/01/2024 as amended by FXD/04/2026
Handle tracking enquiries, errors, reversals and complaints fairly, and turn remittance receivers into account holders
Spot AML/CFT and fraud red flags such as structuring, third-party collection, sanctions matches and romance or job scams, and escalate them correctly

runningCase.name: Eight cases at Bank A's Piassa remittance desk
runningCase.text: Mahlet Tadesse runs the remittance desk at Bank A's Piassa branch in Addis Ababa, with supervisor Dereje Alemu and branch compliance officer Rahel Kassa. Over one busy week she handles eight cases: Almaz Kebede collecting USD 300 from her son in Washington; Aster Belay, aged 72, who arrives with no ID; Tigist Alemayehu, whose USD 600 from Jeddah is too large for her wallet; Bekele Tsegaye, who wants to send USD 2,500 to his sister in Nairobi; Selam Girma from Toronto, who opens a USD diaspora account; Mulugeta Abebe, who was paid at the wrong rate; Yared Hailu, who receives nine transfers from seven senders in 12 days; and Hana Worku, who receives USD 1,500 from an online friend she has never met. Each module works through some of the cases, and the last lesson brings all eight together. Exchange rates in the cases are illustrative: Bank A's buying rate is Birr 152.40 per USD and its selling rate is Birr 155.50 per USD.

modules.title: Remittances and Ethiopia
modules.summary: Why remittances matter to Ethiopian households and to the country's foreign exchange, where they come from, and why informal channels shrank after the July 2024 reform.
objectives: Define inward and outward remittances and the parties to a transfer
Name the main sending corridors and the kinds of senders in each
Explain why remittances matter for households and for the banking system's FX supply
Explain why many families used informal channels and why that changed after July 2024

lessons.title: What a remittance is
body: A remittance is money that a person working or living abroad sends to family or friends at home. An inward remittance comes into Ethiopia; an outward remittance leaves it. Every transfer has a sender, a beneficiary (the receiver), and at least one provider in between: a money transfer operator (MTO), a bank, a wallet provider or, outside the law, an informal broker.

For the receiving family the money is often a lifeline. It pays for food, rent, school fees and medical bills, and it is often saved to build a house or start a small business. For the bank, each formal transfer brings foreign currency into the banking system and a customer to the counter.
points: Sender: the person abroad who pays the money in
Beneficiary: the person in Ethiopia who receives it
Provider: the MTO, bank or wallet that moves and pays the money
Payout agent: the bank branch, agent or wallet that hands it over

items.label: Daily needs
items.text: Food, rent and utility bills

items.label: Education
items.text: School and university fees

items.label: Health
items.text: Medical bills and medicines

items.label: Housing
items.text: Building or improving a home

items.label: Business
items.text: Capital for a small shop or farm

items.label: Savings
items.text: A buffer for hard times

example.title: Running case, case 1: Almaz Kebede
example.text: Almaz Kebede, a widow in Addis Ababa, receives USD 300 every month from her son Henok, a nurse in Washington. She uses it for rent, her medicines and her granddaughter's school fees. Henok sends it through an MTO for which Bank A's Piassa branch is a payout agent, and Almaz collects it from Mahlet Tadesse at the remittance desk.

lessons.tip: Treat every remittance customer as a family's budget in your hands: accuracy and courtesy matter as much as speed.

lessons.title: Where the money comes from
body: Most remittances to Ethiopia come through a few corridors. The United States has a large, long-settled Ethiopian community of professionals, drivers, nurses and business owners. The Gulf states, especially Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, host many Ethiopian workers in domestic work, construction and services. Europe and South Africa add further flows, with South Africa important for traders and workers from the south of the country.

Each corridor behaves differently. United States senders often send larger, regular amounts and are comfortable with apps and bank accounts. Gulf workers often send smaller amounts, close to payday, and many use cash agents near where they live. Knowing the corridor helps you expect what a normal transfer looks like, and spot one that does not fit.

items.label: United States
items.text: Settled diaspora; regular, larger transfers; apps and accounts

items.label: Gulf states
items.text: Migrant workers; smaller, payday transfers; cash agents

items.label: Europe
items.text: Professionals and students; mixed channels

items.label: South Africa
items.text: Traders and workers; cash and informal links

example.title: Two senders, two patterns
example.text: Kidist Mengistu works as a housemaid in Riyadh and sends about USD 150 to her parents in Hosaena on the 28th of each month through a cash agent near her employer's home. Dawit Haile, an IT engineer in Seattle, sends USD 1,200 every quarter from his phone, straight into his mother's account in Bahir Dar. Both are normal for their corridor.

lessons.title: Why remittances matter for foreign exchange
body: Ethiopia needs foreign currency to pay for fuel, medicines, machinery and other imports. Remittances are one of the country's largest sources of that currency, alongside exports, aid and foreign investment. When a transfer is paid out through a bank, the beneficiary receives Birr and the foreign currency stays in the banking system, where importers and other customers can buy it.

When the same money moves informally, the family may still receive Birr, but the dollars stay abroad with a broker and are often used to pay for goods brought in outside the banking system. The country loses FX supply, and the family loses the protection of a regulated provider.

visual.caption: The family gets Birr; the dollars stay in Ethiopia's banking system.

scenario.title: A customer asks why it matters
scenario.situation: While collecting USD 200, Kebede Worku asks Mahlet why the bank cares whether he uses the desk or a broker his neighbor recommends. He receives the same Birr either way, he says.
scenario.question: Which answer is accurate and helpful?
options: There is no difference; the bank just wants the commission
Brokers are fine as long as the amount is small
The bank will report him to the police if he uses a broker
Through the bank his money is protected by a regulated provider and the dollars stay in Ethiopia's banking system, where they pay for imports such as fuel and medicines
scenario.explain: The formal channel protects the family and adds to the country's FX supply. Threats or false claims are not good service, and informal FX dealing is not legal at any size.

lessons.title: Informal channels and why people used them
body: Informal transfer systems, often called hawala, work on trust between brokers. The sender gives cash to a broker abroad; a partner broker in Ethiopia pays the family in Birr; the brokers settle among themselves later, often through trade. No money crosses the border through a bank, and there is usually no record a family could use to claim a lost payment.

Before July 2024, many families used these channels because the parallel market paid far more Birr per dollar than the official rate. Brokers were also fast, reached remote villages and needed no paperwork. The cost was hidden: no protection against loss or fraud, exposure to money laundering, and dealing in foreign currency outside the law.

left.title: Formal channel (bank, MTO, wallet)
items: Regulated by the NBE
Tracking number and receipt
Refund or claim if something goes wrong
Customer identified and screened
Dollars stay in the banking system

right.title: Informal channel (hawala broker)
items: Outside the law for FX dealing
No record a family can rely on
No remedy if the broker disappears
Open to money laundering and fraud
Dollars stay abroad

regulation.source: National Bank of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 1359/2025, Art. 39
regulation.text: Foreign exchange may be dealt in only through banks and dealers authorized by the NBE. Buying or selling foreign currency through an unlicensed broker, at home or abroad, is outside the law.

lessons.title: What changed after July 2024
body: On 29 July 2024, FXD/01/2024 moved Ethiopia to a market-based exchange rate. Banks now buy and sell foreign currency at rates they negotiate freely, and the NBE publishes only an indicative daily rate. As bank rates moved toward the market, the gap between the bank rate and the parallel rate narrowed, so the main reason to use a broker weakened.

Banks, MTOs and wallet providers then competed harder for remittances, with faster payout, wallet credit and better service. FXD/04/2026, in force from 12 February 2026, relaxed further rules, including removing the minimum deposit on FX accounts. For the desk, this means more customers, more digital channels and higher expectations.

items.label: Before July 2024
items.text: Official rate far below the parallel rate; many families use brokers

items.label: 29 July 2024
items.text: FXD/01/2024: freely negotiated rates, NBE indicative rate
Gap narrows; banks, MTOs and wallets compete for remittances

items.label: 12 February 2026
items.text: FXD/04/2026 relaxes FX account and outward transfer rules

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. FXD/01/2024, Foreign exchange (in force 29 July 2024)
regulation.text: Banks buy and sell foreign currency at freely negotiated rates, and the NBE publishes a non-binding indicative rate. The directive also sets the rules for foreign currency accounts, including accounts for non-resident Ethiopians and foreign nationals of Ethiopian origin.

scenario.title: A better rate in Dubai
scenario.situation: Tigist Alemayehu tells Mahlet that her brother in Dubai was offered Birr 154.00 per USD by a broker, against Bank A's buying rate of Birr 152.40. She asks whether he should switch for his next USD 600.
scenario.question: What is the best response?
options: Explain the formal channel's protection and the legal risk, show that the gap is now small, and mention faster wallet or account payout through the bank
Agree, because the broker pays about Birr 960 more
Offer to match the broker's rate from the desk
Tell her the bank rate is fixed by the NBE and cannot change
scenario.explain: The gap is about 1%, while the broker offers no protection and deals outside the law. The desk cannot set its own rate, and bank rates are no longer fixed by the NBE.

lessons.title: The running case: a week at the Piassa desk
body: Throughout this course you will work alongside Mahlet Tadesse at Bank A's Piassa branch. She pays out MTO transfers, credits SWIFT transfers to accounts, helps customers send money abroad and opens diaspora accounts. Her supervisor Dereje Alemu authorizes payments above her limit, and Rahel Kassa handles anything suspicious.

Mahlet's eight cases cover the situations you will meet most often: a routine payout, a customer without ID, a wallet limit, an outward transfer, a diaspora account, an error, a suspicious series of transfers and a likely scam. Before each decision, ask three questions: who is this customer, what does the rule say, and does this transaction make sense?

worked.title: What Almaz's family receives: formal or informal (illustrative)

rows.label: Through the MTO, at Bank A's buying rate of Birr 152.40
Protection if the money is lost
rows.value: MTO: claim and refund; broker: none

rows.label: Legal status
rows.value: MTO: licensed; broker: FX dealing outside the law

worked.note: Once the rate gap is small, the extra Birr rarely pays for the risk of losing the whole transfer.

lessons.tip: Keep the day's rate sheet visible at the desk so you can show customers the rate, not just tell them.

takeaways: A remittance has a sender, a beneficiary and a regulated provider in between; the payout agent is the face the family sees.
The main corridors are the United States, the Gulf, Europe and South Africa, and each has its own normal pattern.
Formal transfers keep foreign currency in Ethiopia's banking system, where it pays for imports.
Informal brokers offer no protection and deal in FX outside the law under Proclamation No. 1359/2025, Art. 39.
FXD/01/2024 narrowed the gap between bank and parallel rates, which made formal channels more attractive.

quiz.q: Which party hands the money to the family in Ethiopia?
quiz.explain: The payout agent, such as a bank branch, agent or wallet, pays the beneficiary.

quiz.q: When a remittance is paid out through a bank, what happens to the foreign currency?
options: It stays in Ethiopia's banking system
It is returned to the sender
It is paid to the beneficiary in dollars by law
quiz.explain: The beneficiary receives Birr while the FX stays in the banking system.

quiz.q: Why did many families use informal brokers before July 2024?
options: Brokers were licensed by the NBE
The parallel market paid far more Birr per dollar
quiz.explain: The large gap between official and parallel rates was the main draw.

quiz.q: Under FXD/01/2024, how are bank buying and selling rates set?
options: Freely negotiated, with an NBE indicative rate
Set by the Ministry of Finance
quiz.explain: Rates are freely negotiated; the NBE rate is indicative and non-binding.

quiz.q: A transfer of USD 400 is paid at Birr 152.40. How much Birr does the beneficiary receive?
Which statement about a typical Gulf-corridor transfer is most accurate?
options: Usually large quarterly amounts sent by app
Often smaller amounts close to payday, frequently through cash agents
quiz.explain: Many Gulf workers send smaller payday amounts through cash agents.

modules.title: Channels and players
modules.summary: How MTOs, bank-to-bank SWIFT transfers, wallets and agents move money into Ethiopia, and how to choose the right payout channel for each customer.
objectives: Describe how an MTO transfer moves from sender to payout
Explain a SWIFT transfer, correspondent banks and the OUR, SHA and BEN charge options
Explain wallet payout and the wallet limits that apply
Describe the role of agents and the NBE approval behind agency agreements
Match a customer's needs to cash, account or wallet payout

lessons.title: The map of channels
body: Money reaches Ethiopia through four formal routes. MTOs collect cash or card payments abroad and pay out through Ethiopian banks and their agents. Banks send SWIFT transfers to each other through correspondent accounts. Wallet providers credit a mobile wallet directly. Agents, such as retail shops working for a bank, extend payout to places with no branch.

Many transfers combine routes: an app abroad may collect the money, an MTO may route it, and an Ethiopian bank may credit it to a wallet. What matters at the desk is who instructed the payment, who the beneficiary is and through which system the money arrives.

items.label: Sender pays in
items.text: Cash at an agent abroad, card or app

items.label: Tracking number issued
items.text: The sender passes it to the beneficiary

items.label: Transfer available
items.text: Appears in the payout system of the Ethiopian bank

items.label: Beneficiary identified
items.text: ID, tracking number, sender name and amount checked

items.label: Payout
items.text: Cash, account credit or wallet, in Birr

items.label: Settlement
items.text: The MTO settles the bank in foreign currency

lessons.title: Money transfer operators
body: MTOs specialize in person-to-person transfers. Global networks such as Western Union, MoneyGram and Ria have agents in most countries; digital operators such as WorldRemit work mainly through apps; operators such as Dahabshiil grew by serving East African communities. In Ethiopia, MTOs pay out through licensed banks, which act as their agents.

Each transfer carries a tracking number, often called a control or reference number. The sender gives it to the beneficiary, and the payout officer uses it to find the transfer. The MTO settles with the paying bank in foreign currency, and the bank earns a share of the commission and the FX it buys.

items.label: Global networks
items.text: Western Union, MoneyGram, Ria

items.label: Digital operators
items.text: WorldRemit and app-based services

items.label: Community operators
items.text: Dahabshiil and others serving the region

items.label: Ethiopian bank
items.text: Licensed payout agent and FX buyer

example.title: Running case, case 1: Almaz collects
example.text: Almaz Kebede gives Mahlet the tracking number Henok sent her by text, says the sender is Henok Kebede in Washington and that she expects USD 300. Mahlet finds the transfer, the details match, and Almaz shows her Fayda ID. Mahlet pays Birr 45,720 at the buying rate of Birr 152.40, and Almaz signs the payout receipt.

lessons.tip: Never read the sender's name or the amount aloud first. Ask the customer to tell you, then compare.

lessons.title: Bank-to-bank SWIFT transfers
body: A sender can also ask a bank abroad to transfer money to an account at an Ethiopian bank. The banks exchange a SWIFT customer transfer message (an MT103, or its ISO 20022 equivalent) that names the ordering customer, the beneficiary, the beneficiary's account and the purpose. If the two banks do not hold accounts with each other, the money passes through a correspondent bank, and the Ethiopian bank receives it in its nostro account abroad.

The sender chooses who pays the charges. With OUR, the sender pays all charges and the full amount arrives. With SHA, the sender pays the sending bank, and correspondent charges are deducted on the way. With BEN, all charges come out of the amount. Explaining this saves many complaints about money that "went missing".

worked.title: A SHA transfer from Toronto (illustrative)

rows.label: Amount Selam's bank in Toronto sends
Amount received in Bank A's nostro account
If credited in Birr at Birr 152.40
If credited to her USD diaspora account

worked.note: The USD 20 difference is a correspondent charge under SHA, not an error by the desk. Show the customer the incoming message details.

scenario.title: Twenty dollars missing
scenario.situation: Selam Girma's brother complains that USD 1,000 was sent from Canada but only USD 980 reached the account. The incoming message shows charge option SHA and a USD 20 deduction by the correspondent bank.
scenario.question: What should the desk tell him?
options: The sender chose SHA, so the correspondent bank deducted its charge on the way; choosing OUR next time would deliver the full amount
Bank A will refund USD 20 at once
The money was stolen and he should call the police
The NBE took a USD 20 tax
scenario.explain: Under SHA, correspondent charges are deducted from the amount. OUR makes the sender pay all charges so the full amount arrives.

lessons.title: Wallet payout
body: Many remittances now go straight to a mobile wallet such as telebirr, M-PESA or a bank's own wallet. The family receives Birr on the phone in minutes, with no trip to a branch. The legal basis is the National Payment System Proclamation No. 718/2011 as amended by No. 1282/2023, and the NBE's directives on payment instrument issuers.

Wallets have limits. The ONPS/09/2023 directive, as reported, set a daily wallet balance limit of Birr 75,000 and a daily aggregate transaction limit of Birr 150,000. A large remittance may therefore not fit in a wallet. Check the current limits, because the issuer rules were amended again by ONPS/10/2025.

regulation.source: National Payment System Proclamation No. 718/2011, amended by No. 1282/2023, and NBE Directive No. ONPS/09/2023 (as reported; further amended by ONPS/10/2025)
regulation.text: Payment instrument issuers, including mobile money providers and bank subsidiaries, operate under NBE licensing. ONPS/09/2023 is reported to set a daily wallet balance limit of Birr 75,000 and a daily aggregate transaction limit of Birr 150,000, with some exemptions. Confirm the current limits with your bank.

scenario.title: Running case, case 5: too big for the wallet
scenario.situation: Tigist Alemayehu's brother in Jeddah wants to send USD 600 to her wallet. At Birr 152.40 that is Birr 91,440, and she already holds about Birr 5,000 in the wallet.
scenario.question: What should Mahlet advise?
options: Send it to the wallet; limits do not apply to remittances
Receive it into a Bank A account, which has no wallet balance limit, and move smaller amounts to the wallet as needed
Split it into two transfers on the same day
Ask the brother to use a broker
scenario.explain: Birr 91,440 is above the reported Birr 75,000 balance limit. An account credit fits the rule; splitting to get around a limit is a red flag.

lessons.title: Agents and agency agreements
body: A bank pays out MTO transfers as the MTO's agent under an agency agreement. The NBE regulates these arrangements: international money transfer operators and their agency agreements with Ethiopian banks need NBE approval under its rules on money transfer services. The directive number for these rules should be confirmed from the bank's compliance unit.

Banks also appoint their own agents, such as shops and cooperatives, to serve customers where there is no branch. An agent acts for the bank and must follow the same identification, limit and record rules. If an agent breaks them, the bank carries the risk.

example.title: An agent in Debre Markos
example.text: Bank A's agent in Debre Markos, Getnet Ayele, runs a stationery shop and pays out small remittances on a tablet linked to the bank. A customer asks him to pay his cousin's transfer because the cousin is sick at home. Getnet refuses politely and explains that the named beneficiary must come with ID, or open an account so the money can be credited.

scenario.title: An agent who wants to help
scenario.situation: Bank A's area office notices that one agent pays out many transfers to people whose ID numbers are all written by hand on the receipts, with no scanned copy. The agent says the customers are farmers who forget their IDs.
scenario.question: What should the bank do?
options: Nothing, because the agent knows the community
Raise the agent's commission to reward the volume
Stop the agent's payouts pending review, check the transactions and retrain or end the agency if rules were broken
Ask the agent to scan IDs from now on and ignore the past
scenario.explain: The agent acts for the bank, so the bank must review past payouts and act; payouts without verified ID are a compliance and fraud risk.

lessons.title: Choosing the payout channel
body: A good desk officer helps each family choose how to receive money. Cash suits customers who need it at once and have no account. An account credit is safer, keeps a record, earns interest and lets the family build a history with the bank. A wallet is fastest and works far from a branch, within its limits.

Think about the amount, how often money comes, where the beneficiary lives and whether they can read and use a phone. Elderly customers, for example, may prefer cash at the branch with a relative present, while a student may want wallet credit.

left.title: Cash at the counter
items: Immediate, no account needed
Customer must travel and carry cash
Risk of theft after leaving
No savings habit built

right.title: Account or wallet credit
items: Safer and recorded
Can be received far from a branch
Builds a relationship and a savings habit
Wallet credits are capped by wallet limits

example.title: Choosing for Almaz
example.text: After three months of cash payouts, Mahlet suggests that Almaz Kebede open a savings account so Henok's USD 300 is credited directly. Almaz no longer queues each month, and she keeps Birr 5,000 aside each time toward her granddaughter's university fees.

takeaways: Formal routes are MTOs, SWIFT bank transfers, wallets and agents, often combined in one transfer.
An MTO transfer is found by its tracking number and must match the sender, amount and beneficiary ID.
Under SHA, correspondent charges reduce the amount received; OUR delivers the full amount.
Wallet payouts must fit wallet limits; reported ONPS/09/2023 limits are Birr 75,000 balance and Birr 150,000 daily transactions.
Agents act for the bank, which carries the risk when they break identification or record rules.

quiz.q: Which SWIFT charge option makes the sender pay all charges so the full amount arrives?
quiz.explain: With OUR, the sender pays every charge.

quiz.q: An MTO transfer is mainly located by:
quiz.explain: The tracking number identifies the transfer in the payout system.

quiz.q: A USD 700 transfer at Birr 152.40 is Birr 106,680. Under the reported ONPS/09/2023 limits, can it all go to a wallet holding Birr 2,000?
options: No, it exceeds the Birr 75,000 balance limit
quiz.explain: The balance would exceed Birr 75,000, so an account credit is needed.

quiz.q: Who carries the risk when a bank's agent pays a transfer without proper ID?
quiz.explain: The agent acts for the bank, so the bank is responsible.

quiz.q: A SHA transfer of USD 2,000 has a USD 25 correspondent charge. What reaches Bank A's nostro?
Which payout channel best builds a long-term relationship with the family?
quiz.explain: An account credit creates a record, a savings habit and a banking relationship.

modules.title: Payout and send procedures
modules.summary: Pay out and send transfers correctly: identification and Fayda, cash, account or wallet payout, conversion at the bank's rate, the 24-hour payout rule, outward eligibility and record keeping.
objectives: Follow the payout steps from tracking number to signed receipt
Identify beneficiaries with Fayda and other acceptable IDs, and handle a customer without ID
Convert at the bank's rate or credit an eligible FCY account
Apply the 24-hour payout and charge rule cited for remittance service providers
Process an outward family support transfer within FXD/04/2026

lessons.title: The payout steps
body: Every payout follows the same order, whatever the channel. The customer gives the tracking number, the sender's name, the sending country and the expected amount. The officer finds the transfer and compares. The customer's original ID is checked against the beneficiary's name, and the person is screened through the bank's system.

Only then is the amount converted and paid, the receipt signed by the customer, and the voucher checked by a second person where the amount needs it. Skipping a step to save time is how most payout losses happen.

items.label: Ask, do not tell
items.text: Tracking number, sender, country and amount from the customer

items.label: Match the transfer
items.text: All details agree with the payout system

items.label: Verify the ID
items.text: Original, valid, name matches, photo matches the person

items.label: Screen
items.text: Sanctions and internal watch lists

items.label: Convert and pay
items.text: Cash, account or wallet at the day's rate

items.label: Sign and check
items.text: Customer signs; checker countersigns where required

items.label: Record
items.text: ID copy, receipt and voucher filed

lessons.tip: If any detail does not match, stop and ask your supervisor before paying. A paid transfer is very hard to recover.

lessons.title: Identification and Fayda
body: The beneficiary must present a valid original ID. Fayda, the national digital ID, lets the bank confirm identity against the national register, which reduces fraud with fake paper IDs. Other IDs the bank accepts, such as a kebele ID, passport or driving licence, must be valid, unaltered and in the same name as the transfer.

Small spelling differences are common because names are transliterated from Amharic or Afaan Oromo, for example Abebe and Abebbe. Your bank's procedure will say which differences a supervisor may accept and which need the sender to amend the transfer. A different person, an expired ID or no ID means no payout.

regulation.source: NBE KYC/CDD directive (2021, number to confirm) and the AML/CFT law
regulation.text: Banks must identify and verify every customer, including occasional customers who only collect a transfer, keep a copy of the ID and the transaction record, and apply enhanced checks where the risk is higher.

scenario.title: Running case, case 2: no ID
scenario.situation: Aster Belay, 72, comes from a village near Sodo with her grandson to collect USD 200 from her daughter in Dubai. She knows the tracking number and the sender, but she has no ID card. Her grandson shows his own Fayda ID and offers to collect for her.
scenario.question: What should Mahlet do?
options: Pay the grandson because he has a valid ID
Pay Aster because the details match and she is clearly elderly
Not pay today; explain kindly that Aster needs a valid ID, help her with Fayda registration, and keep the transfer available or ask the sender to change the beneficiary
Cancel the transfer and refund the sender at once
scenario.explain: The named beneficiary must be identified, and paying a third party breaks the rule. Kindness means helping her get an ID, not skipping the check; the transfer stays available while she does.

lessons.title: Cash, account or wallet payout
body: Cash payout is counted in front of the customer, with large amounts authorized under the bank's limits. An account credit goes to an account in the beneficiary's own name; never credit a third party's account because the customer asks. A wallet credit goes to a wallet registered in the beneficiary's name and must fit the wallet limits.
For larger cash amounts, offer an account. A customer walking out of Piassa with Birr 200,000 in a plastic bag is at risk, and the branch has a duty to suggest the safer choice.

example.title: A large cash payout
example.text: Fikru Desta comes to collect USD 1,800 from his brother in Minneapolis, Birr 274,320 at Birr 152.40. Mahlet passes the payment to Dereje Alemu for authorization because it is above her limit, and suggests that Fikru open a savings account and take only the cash he needs. Fikru takes Birr 50,000 in cash and leaves the rest in a new account.

items.label: Cash
items.text: Count in front of the customer; authorize above limits

items.label: Account credit
items.text: Only to the beneficiary's own account

items.label: Wallet credit
items.text: Beneficiary's own wallet, within limits

lessons.title: Conversion at the bank's rate
body: Inward remittances to residents are normally paid in Birr at the bank's buying rate on the day of payout. Under FXD/01/2024, banks set this rate freely, so it can differ between banks and from the NBE indicative rate. Always use the rate in the system and show it on the receipt.

Where the beneficiary holds an eligible foreign currency account, such as a diaspora account, the transfer may be credited in foreign currency instead of being converted. The account must be eligible to receive that credit under FXD/01/2024 as amended and the bank's product rules.

worked.title: Running case, case 1: Almaz's payout and the charge check

rows.label: Maximum charge at 1% (rule cited in the specification)
Time from transfer available to payout

worked.note: Check the rate, the amount and any charge before the customer signs; correcting a paid transfer later needs a reversal.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. FXD/01/2024, as amended by FXD/04/2026
regulation.text: Banks buy foreign currency at freely negotiated rates. Remittance proceeds are converted to Birr at the bank's rate or credited to a foreign currency account where the account holder is eligible. FXD/04/2026 removed the minimum deposit on foreign currency accounts.

lessons.title: Pay within 24 hours, charge at most 1%
body: The course specification cites Article 11 of the NBE rules on remittance service providers: providers must pay beneficiaries within 24 hours and may charge at most 1%. Confirm the exact text and the base for the 1% with your compliance unit, because the directive number is still to be confirmed.

In practice, the desk must not hold an available transfer without a reason, and must not add charges outside the bank's published tariff. A transfer held for a compliance reason, such as a name mismatch or a screening alert, should be recorded with the reason and the time.

regulation.source: NBE rules on remittance service providers, Art. 11, as cited in Erudite's course specification (directive number to confirm)
regulation.text: Remittance service providers must pay beneficiaries within 24 hours and may charge at most 1%.

scenario.title: Come back next week
scenario.situation: A busy Monday at Piassa. A colleague tells Meseret Ali, who has a valid Fayda ID and a matching USD 250 transfer, to come back on Thursday because the desk is full, and suggests a Birr 500 "service fee" to serve her today.
scenario.question: What is the right action?
options: Accept the arrangement; the desk is busy
Ask Meseret to pay half the fee
Serve Meseret today at the published tariff only, and report the fee request to the supervisor
scenario.explain: A matching transfer with valid ID must be paid promptly, and charges outside the tariff are not allowed. Asking for an unofficial fee is misconduct and must be reported.

lessons.title: Sending money abroad
body: Outward transfers use the bank's own foreign currency, so they must fit the purposes allowed by FXD/01/2024 as amended. FXD/04/2026 allows residents to send up to USD 3,000 abroad for family support. Check the documents your bank requires, the period over which the limit is counted, and the purpose code for the transfer.

The customer pays in Birr at the bank's selling rate plus the bank's tariff, and the bank sends a SWIFT transfer or uses an MTO send service. Check the source of the Birr for larger amounts, screen the beneficiary, and keep the purpose and supporting documents on file. Other purposes, such as imports or dividends, follow their own sections of the directive.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. FXD/04/2026, amending FXD/01/2024 (in force 12 February 2026)
regulation.text: Residents may send up to USD 3,000 abroad for family support. Banks may also approve dividend remittances and external loans without NBE approval, with monthly reporting, and outward investment is allowed case by case with NBE approval.

worked.title: Running case, case 6: Bekele's transfer to Nairobi

rows.label: Purpose
rows.value: Family support to his sister, a resident of Kenya

rows.label: Amount requested
rows.value: USD 2,500 (within the USD 3,000 family support limit)

rows.label: Plus
rows.value: Bank A's tariff for outward transfers

rows.label: Checks
rows.value: Bekele's ID, source of Birr, beneficiary screened, earlier family support transfers in the period

worked.note: If Bekele had already sent USD 1,000 for family support in the same period, a USD 2,500 transfer would take him above USD 3,000 and could not be processed under this purpose.

scenario.title: A second transfer
scenario.situation: Two weeks after the Nairobi transfer, Bekele Tsegaye returns and asks to send another USD 1,500 to the same sister for family support, within the same period.
scenario.question: What should Mahlet do?
options: Explain that USD 2,500 plus USD 1,500 exceeds the USD 3,000 family support limit for the period, and offer USD 500 at most
Process it, because each transfer is below USD 3,000
Process it in his wife's name to stay under the limit
Send it through an MTO so the limit does not apply
scenario.explain: The limit is counted per person over the period, so only USD 500 remains. Using another person's name or another channel to get around it is structuring.

lessons.title: Record keeping
body: For every payout or send, the bank keeps the customer's ID copy, the signed receipt, the voucher with maker and checker, the rate used, and for outward transfers the purpose and documents. These records let the bank answer customer claims, reconcile with the MTO and respond to the NBE and the Financial Intelligence Service.
Keep records for the period the AML/CFT law and the bank's policy require, file them the same day, and never keep customer ID copies on a personal phone.
points: ID copy or Fayda verification result
Signed payout or send receipt showing the rate
Screening result and any hold reason
Purpose and documents for outward transfers

example.title: A claim six months later
example.text: An MTO queries a USD 400 transfer paid at Piassa in April, because the sender claims his mother never received it. Mahlet pulls the file: the Fayda verification, the signed receipt and the countersigned voucher. The MTO closes the claim the same day.

takeaways: Ask the customer for the tracking number, sender and amount, then compare; never read the details out first.
Pay only the named beneficiary on a valid original ID; no ID or a third party means no payout.
Convert at the bank's buying rate, or credit an eligible FCY account, and show the rate on the receipt.
The specification cites a 24-hour payout rule and a 1% charge cap for remittance service providers (directive number to confirm).
FXD/04/2026 allows residents to send up to USD 3,000 abroad for family support; count earlier transfers in the period.
File the ID, receipt, voucher and screening result the same day.

quiz.q: What should the payout officer do first?
options: Read the sender's name to the customer
Ask the customer for the tracking number, sender and expected amount
quiz.explain: The customer must give the details so the officer can compare them.

quiz.q: A beneficiary's son offers his own valid ID to collect for his mother. The bank should:
options: Not pay; the named beneficiary must be identified
quiz.explain: Only the named beneficiary may collect, on a valid ID.

quiz.q: USD 850 is paid at Birr 152.40. What does the beneficiary receive?
Under FXD/04/2026, how much may a resident send abroad for family support?
quiz.explain: FXD/04/2026 allows up to USD 3,000 for family support.

quiz.q: At a selling rate of Birr 155.50, how much Birr does a USD 2,000 family support transfer cost before tariff?
Which record is NOT needed on a payout file?
options: The ID copy or Fayda result
The signed receipt with the rate
quiz.explain: A salary slip is not part of a routine payout file; ID, receipt and voucher are.

modules.title: Customer service
modules.summary: Track transfers, correct errors through proper reversals, handle cancellations and complaints fairly, open diaspora FCY accounts and turn remittance receivers into long-term customers.
objectives: Explain a transfer's status and answer tracking enquiries
Correct payout errors through a controlled reversal
Handle cancellations, refunds and complaints under consumer protection rules
Open a diaspora FCY account correctly
Cross-sell accounts and wallets to remittance receivers

lessons.title: Tracking numbers and transfer status
body: Many visits to the desk are status questions: has the money arrived? The tracking number tells you the status in the payout system. A transfer may be sent but not yet available, available for payout, on hold for a compliance check, paid, or cancelled and refunded to the sender.

Give customers only what they need: whether the money is available and what to bring. Never share the sender's details or the amount with someone who cannot already tell you them, because fraudsters use status enquiries to learn about transfers.

items.label: Sent
items.text: Paid in abroad; tracking number issued

items.label: Available
items.text: Ready for payout in the Ethiopian bank's system

items.label: On hold
items.text: Compliance or detail check; reason recorded

items.label: Paid
items.text: Beneficiary identified and paid; receipt signed

items.label: Cancelled
items.text: Refunded to the sender before payout

example.title: A caller asks about a transfer
example.text: A man phones Piassa and says he is calling for his aunt, who is expecting money from Riyadh. He gives a tracking number and asks for the amount and the sender's name. Mahlet says only that the beneficiary should come to the branch with her ID and the details from the sender, and gives no amount or name.

lessons.title: Errors and reversals
body: Errors happen: the wrong rate keyed, a transfer paid twice, or money credited to the wrong account. Once a transaction is committed, it is corrected only by a reversal and a new correct entry, made by one person and checked by another, with the reason written on the voucher. Nobody edits a posted transaction or settles a difference from their own pocket.
Tell the customer what happened, what the bank will do and when. A short apology and a clear correction keep trust; hiding an error damages it.

worked.title: Running case, case 7: Mulugeta paid at the wrong rate

rows.label: Correction
rows.value: Reverse the Birr 50,160 entry, post Birr 60,960, pay the Birr 10,800 difference against a signed receipt

rows.label: Control
rows.value: Maker and checker on the reversal, reason recorded, supervisor informed

worked.note: The receipt Mulugeta signed showed Birr 125.40, which is how he spotted the error. Showing the rate on every receipt protects both sides.

scenario.title: A colleague offers a shortcut
scenario.situation: At day end Mahlet's till is Birr 10,800 over because Mulugeta Abebe was underpaid. A colleague suggests she simply hand Mulugeta the Birr 10,800 from the till when he comes back, with no entries, to avoid paperwork.
scenario.question: What should Mahlet do?
options: Report the overage, reverse the wrong entry and post the correct one with maker and checker, then pay Mulugeta against a signed receipt
Follow the suggestion; the till will balance
Keep the surplus in the till until month end
Ask Mulugeta to accept the lower amount
scenario.explain: Committed transactions are corrected only by a controlled reversal and a correct entry. Off-book cash payments hide errors and invite fraud.

lessons.title: Cancellations and refunds
body: A sender may cancel a transfer that has not been paid. The MTO or sending bank cancels it and refunds the sender abroad; the Ethiopian desk does not refund in Birr. Once a transfer is paid to a properly identified beneficiary, it cannot be cancelled by the sender, and any dispute is between sender and beneficiary.

If a sender says a transfer was paid to the wrong person, the bank checks its file. If the ID was verified correctly, the bank shows its records; if the bank paid without proper checks, it may have to make good the loss, which is why the payout steps matter.

scenario.title: A sender changes her mind
scenario.situation: A woman in Abu Dhabi calls Piassa saying she sent USD 500 to her ex-husband by mistake and wants it stopped. The transfer is still available, not paid.
scenario.question: What should the desk tell her?
options: The desk will block it and pay it to her mother instead
She should ask the MTO or agent where she sent it to cancel it; once cancelled, it is refunded to her there
Nothing can be done once a transfer is sent
The ex-husband must agree before it can be cancelled
scenario.explain: The sender cancels through the sending MTO or bank, and the refund is made where she paid. The desk cannot redirect a transfer on a phone call.

lessons.title: Handling complaints
body: Remittance complaints are often about delays, rates, charges or refused payouts. Ethiopian consumer protection rules require fair treatment, clear disclosure and proper complaint handling. NBE Proclamation No. 1359/2025 gives the NBE consumer protection powers, and the NBE's financial consumer protection directive, FCP/01/2020 (as reported), sets out how banks must treat and answer customers.

Listen, record the complaint, explain the rule in plain words, and give a time for an answer. When the bank is wrong, correct it quickly. When the customer is refused for a rule, such as missing ID, say what they can do next.

regulation.source: NBE Proclamation No. 1359/2025, Art. 41, and NBE Directive No. FCP/01/2020 (as reported)
regulation.text: Banks must treat financial consumers fairly, disclose prices and charges clearly, protect customer data and run a complaint handling process that records, answers and escalates complaints.

items.label: Listen
items.text: Let the customer explain without interrupting

items.label: Record
items.text: Log the complaint with a reference number

items.label: Check
items.text: Pull the transfer file and the rule that applies

items.label: Answer
items.text: Explain plainly and give a time for any fix

items.label: Escalate
items.text: Unresolved cases go to the complaint unit

lessons.title: Opening a diaspora FCY account
body: FXD/01/2024 lets non-resident Ethiopians and foreign nationals of Ethiopian origin open foreign currency accounts. The customer proves identity and status, such as an Ethiopian passport with residence abroad, or a foreign passport with proof of Ethiopian origin, and gives contact details abroad. Since FXD/04/2026 there is no minimum deposit.

A diaspora FCY account must be funded from foreign sources: transfers from abroad, or cash brought in and declared as the rules require. A credit from a local Birr source is not allowed and must be reversed. The account can then receive remittances and later support savings, investment and diaspora loans.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. FXD/01/2024 (FCY accounts for non-resident Ethiopians and foreign nationals of Ethiopian origin), as amended by FXD/04/2026
regulation.text: Non-resident Ethiopians and foreign nationals of Ethiopian origin may hold foreign currency accounts funded from foreign sources. FXD/04/2026 removed the minimum deposit for FX accounts.

example.title: Running case, case 4: Selam Girma opens an account
example.text: Selam Girma, a Canadian citizen born in Gondar, visits Addis Ababa and opens a USD diaspora account at Piassa with her Canadian passport, her Ethiopian origin document and her Toronto address. She funds it with USD 5,000 by SWIFT from her Toronto bank and asks for her brother to receive Birr transfers from the account. Mahlet explains the account rules and links online banking so Selam can send to her brother from Canada.

scenario.title: A local deposit into the diaspora account
scenario.situation: A month later, Selam's brother brings Birr 300,000 from the sale of a car and asks the desk to convert it and credit Selam's USD diaspora account.
scenario.question: What should the desk do?
options: Convert at the selling rate and credit the account
Credit it if Selam approves by email
Decline, because a diaspora FCY account may be funded only from foreign sources; offer a Birr account instead
scenario.explain: Local Birr cannot fund a diaspora FCY account. A Birr account in the right name is the correct alternative.

lessons.title: Turning receivers into customers
body: Every remittance receiver who walks in is a potential long-term customer. A savings account for direct credit, a wallet linked to that account, and a debit card turn a monthly visit into a banking relationship. Families who receive regularly are often good savers and, in time, good borrowers.

Offer, do not push. Explain the benefit in the customer's terms, such as no queue, a safer way to hold money, or saving for school fees, and open the account on the spot if the customer agrees. Track how many payout customers you convert.

visual.caption: Piassa desk payouts by channel in September 2026 (illustrative running case data). The desk's goal is to move more of the cash payouts to account and wallet credit.

example.title: From payout to account holder
example.text: Tigist Alemayehu, from case 5, agrees to open a savings account so her brother's USD 600 can be credited in full. She links her wallet for daily spending and sets aside Birr 10,000 a month for a sewing business. Within a year she asks about a small business loan.

lessons.tip: Ask one simple question at every cash payout: would it be easier if this came straight into an account next time?

takeaways: Share transfer status only with the beneficiary who can give the details; never disclose sender or amount to a caller.
Committed errors are corrected only by a reversal and a correct entry, with maker and checker and a recorded reason.
Unpaid transfers are cancelled by the sender through the sending MTO or bank; paid ones cannot be cancelled.
Handle complaints fairly and on record under Proclamation No. 1359/2025 and FCP/01/2020.
Diaspora FCY accounts are funded only from foreign sources and, since FXD/04/2026, have no minimum deposit.
Each cash payout is a chance to offer an account or wallet.

quiz.q: A caller gives a tracking number and asks for the sender's name. The desk should:
options: Give no details and ask the beneficiary to come with ID and the sender's details
quiz.explain: Status enquiries must not reveal transfer details to unverified callers.

quiz.q: A transfer of USD 250 was paid at Birr 125.40 instead of Birr 152.40. How much was the customer underpaid?
How is a committed payout error corrected?
options: Pay the difference from the till off the books
Reverse it and post the correct entry with maker and checker
quiz.explain: Only a controlled reversal and a new correct entry may correct a posted transaction.

quiz.q: Which deposit may be credited to a diaspora FCY account?
options: Birr from the sale of a local car, converted
A SWIFT transfer from the holder's bank abroad
Rent collected in Birr in Addis Ababa
quiz.explain: Diaspora FCY accounts must be funded from foreign sources.

quiz.q: Who cancels an unpaid MTO transfer?
options: The sender, through the sending MTO or agent
The payout bank on a phone call
quiz.explain: The sender cancels where the transfer was sent, and is refunded there.

quiz.q: Which consumer protection duty applies when a customer complains about a remittance charge?
options: Ignore it if the amount is small
Refer the customer to the MTO without recording it
Record it, explain the charge clearly and answer within a stated time
quiz.explain: Fair treatment requires recording, clear explanation and a timely answer.

modules.title: AML/CFT and fraud
modules.summary: Recognize structuring, third-party collection, sanctions matches and romance and job scams in remittance transactions, report suspicion correctly, and process all eight running cases.
objectives: Explain why remittances carry money laundering and terrorist financing risk and what the wire transfer rules require
Recognize structuring and third-party collection
Apply sanctions screening and handle a possible match
Recognize romance and job scams and protect victims
Escalate suspicion without tipping off the customer

lessons.title: Why remittances are a risk
body: Remittances are small, frequent and cross-border, which makes them useful to criminals as well as families. Money from fraud, smuggling or corruption can be broken into many small transfers, and terrorist financing often uses small amounts. The AML/CFT law, Proclamation No. 780/2013 (as reported), requires banks to identify customers, keep records, monitor transactions and report suspicion to the Financial Intelligence Service.

International standards add a wire transfer rule. FATF Recommendation 16 requires the originator's and beneficiary's information to travel with each transfer, so the paying bank can screen it and the authorities can trace it. A transfer with missing sender details should be queried before payout.

regulation.source: Prevention and Suppression of Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism Proclamation No. 780/2013 (as reported), the NBE KYC/CDD directive, and FATF Recommendation 16
regulation.text: Banks must identify customers, keep transaction records, monitor for unusual activity and report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Service. Cross-border wire transfers must carry complete originator and beneficiary information.

items.label: Structuring
items.text: Many small transfers to stay under review levels

items.label: Third-party collection
items.text: Someone collects for another person

items.label: Sanctions
items.text: Sender or receiver on a sanctions list

items.label: Romance scams
items.text: Online partners who ask for or route money

items.label: Job scams
items.text: Fees for jobs abroad that do not exist

items.label: Missing details
items.text: Incomplete sender or beneficiary information

lessons.title: Structuring and splitting
body: Structuring means breaking a large sum into smaller transfers so that none attracts review. Signs include many senders paying one beneficiary, amounts just below an internal review level, several transfers on the same day or week, and a beneficiary whose income and profile do not explain the total.

The officer does not need proof of a crime. The duty is to notice, ask normal questions, record the answers and escalate to compliance. Whether to file a suspicious transaction report is decided by compliance, not at the desk.

worked.title: Running case, case 3: Yared Hailu's transfers

rows.label: Number of transfers
rows.value: 9, from 7 different senders in Dubai and Riyadh

rows.label: Desk action
rows.value: Pay only if details and ID match; refer the pattern to Rahel Kassa in compliance the same day

worked.note: Each transfer looks ordinary; the pattern does not. Over Birr 1.3 million to a student from seven senders, each just under USD 1,000, needs compliance review.

scenario.title: The ninth transfer
scenario.situation: Yared Hailu comes for his ninth transfer in 12 days, USD 950 from a new sender in Dubai. When Mahlet asks who the senders are, he says they are "friends of a friend" paying for phones he will buy and ship to them.
scenario.question: What should Mahlet do?
options: Refuse and tell Yared he is being reported for money laundering
Pay and do nothing, because each transfer is small
Pay if the transfer and ID match, record his explanation, and refer the pattern to compliance without telling him
Ask Yared to bring all seven senders to the branch
scenario.explain: The desk records and escalates; compliance decides on a report. Telling the customer he is being reported is tipping off, which the law forbids.

lessons.title: Third-party collection and money mules
body: Third-party collection happens when the person collecting is not the real recipient: a relative collecting "for" someone, a person who collects many transfers for others, or a beneficiary who hands the cash straight to someone waiting outside. Criminals use such people, called money mules, to move money while staying hidden.

Watch for a person waiting near the desk who takes the cash, a beneficiary who reads the details from a phone sent by someone else, and one phone number used for several beneficiaries. The named beneficiary must collect on their own ID, and any pattern must be escalated.

example.title: The man by the door
example.text: Over a week, three young women collect transfers of about USD 700 each at Piassa. Each reads the tracking number from a message, and each hands the cash to the same man waiting by the door. Mahlet notes the pattern and the times and tells Rahel Kassa, who reviews the transactions and the CCTV and decides on a report.

scenario.title: The same phone number
scenario.situation: In the payout system, Mahlet sees that four different beneficiaries in the past month gave the same phone number, and two of them are collecting today.
scenario.question: What is the best step?
options: Pay today's two normally and refer the shared number and the four transactions to compliance
Ignore it; families often share phones
Refuse all payouts to anyone with that number permanently
Call the number to ask who owns it
scenario.explain: A shared number across unrelated beneficiaries is a mule indicator. Proper identification continues and compliance reviews the pattern; calling the number could tip off the organizer.

lessons.title: Sanctions screening
body: Every sender and beneficiary is screened against sanctions and watch lists before payout or sending. Most alerts are false positives caused by common names. The officer compares date of birth, nationality, address and ID number with the list entry, and does not clear an alert that cannot be ruled out.
A possible true match goes to compliance at once, and the transfer is held without explanation to the customer beyond a neutral "we need a little more time". Never pay first and screen later.

items.label: Screen
items.text: Sender and beneficiary, before payout or sending

items.label: Compare
items.text: Date of birth, nationality, address, ID number

items.label: Clear or refer
items.text: Clear only clear false positives; refer the rest

items.label: Hold
items.text: Possible match held; neutral words to the customer

items.label: Record
items.text: Reason for clearing or referring kept on file

example.title: A common name
example.text: A beneficiary named Mohammed Ali triggers an alert. The list entry is a man born in 1961 of another nationality; the customer is an Ethiopian born in 1998 with a matching Fayda record. Dereje Alemu clears the alert, records the reasons and Mahlet pays.

lessons.title: Romance and job scams
body: In a romance scam, a stranger met online wins the victim's trust, then sends money for the victim to pass on, or asks the victim for money. The victim may become a money mule without knowing it. In a job scam, a fake agent promises work in the Gulf or Europe and asks the victim's family to send fees abroad for visas, tickets or medical checks.

Victims are often embarrassed or in love, so be patient. Ask simple questions: have you met this person, why is the money coming to you, what are you asked to do with it? Explain the risk, record the conversation and refer it to compliance. The NBE has also asked financial institutions to run fraud awareness campaigns for customers.

left.title: Romance scam signs
items: Partner never met in person
Large "gifts" from abroad
Asked to forward money or buy gift cards
Urgency and secrecy

right.title: Job scam signs
items: Job abroad offered through social media
Fees sent to a personal account abroad
No licensed agency or contract
Repeated new fees after the first

scenario.title: Running case, case 8: Hana's online friend
scenario.situation: Hana Worku, 24, collects USD 1,500 (Birr 228,600) sent by "David", an American engineer she met online two months ago. She says he asked her to send most of it to three Birr accounts for "his business partners" and to keep Birr 20,000 for herself.
scenario.question: What should Mahlet do?
options: Pay if the transfer and ID match, explain gently that this is a common mule scheme and that forwarding the money may make her part of a crime, and refer the case to compliance
Pay and wish her well; it is her money
Transfer the money to the three accounts for her
scenario.explain: The transfer is valid, but Hana is likely being used as a mule. Warning her protects her, and compliance decides on a report.

lessons.title: Escalating and reporting suspicion
body: The desk's job is to notice and escalate. Use your bank's internal unusual transaction form, describe facts not feelings, and send it to compliance the same day. Compliance reviews, may ask for more information and decides whether to file a suspicious transaction report with the Financial Intelligence Service.

Never tell the customer that a report is being made or considered. That is tipping off, which the AML/CFT law forbids, and it can let criminals move money before the authorities act. Keep serving the customer normally unless compliance tells you otherwise.

items.label: Notice
items.text: A pattern, a story or a document that does not fit

items.label: Ask normal questions
items.text: Record the answers in the customer's words

items.label: Escalate
items.text: Internal unusual transaction form to compliance, same day

items.label: Compliance decides
items.text: Review and, if suspicious, a report to the Financial Intelligence Service

items.label: Do not tip off
items.text: Serve normally; say nothing about the report

regulation.text: Banks report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Service and must not disclose to the customer or others that a report has been or may be made.

lessons.title: Capstone: the eight Piassa cases
body: Bring the course together by processing all eight of Mahlet's cases. For each, state the decision, the rule and the record you keep. In the classroom version, learners process the eight cases as the practical part of the assessment, alongside a knowledge test.

Notice how often the right answer is neither "pay at once" nor "refuse". Good remittance work means paying genuine families quickly, helping those who cannot yet be paid, and quietly escalating what does not fit.

worked.title: Decision table for the eight cases

rows.label: 1. Almaz Kebede, USD 300 from Washington
rows.value: Pay Birr 45,720 on Fayda ID; offer a savings account

rows.label: 2. Aster Belay, no ID
rows.value: No payout; help with Fayda; keep the transfer available or sender amends

rows.label: 3. Yared Hailu, 9 transfers, USD 8,560
rows.value: Pay matching transfer; refer the pattern to compliance; no tipping off

rows.label: 4. Selam Girma, diaspora account
rows.value: Open USD account, funded from abroad; refuse local Birr credits

rows.label: 5. Tigist Alemayehu, USD 600 to a wallet
rows.value: Birr 91,440 exceeds wallet limit; credit an account instead

rows.label: 6. Bekele Tsegaye, USD 2,500 to Nairobi
rows.value: Process as family support within USD 3,000; second request limited to USD 500

rows.label: 7. Mulugeta Abebe, wrong rate
rows.value: Reverse and repost; pay Birr 10,800 difference with maker and checker

rows.label: 8. Hana Worku, online friend
rows.value: Pay on ID; warn about mule scheme; refer to compliance

worked.note: Every case ends with a record: the ID, the receipt, the reason for any hold and any referral to compliance.

example.title: What changed at Piassa
example.text: After the week, Dereje Alemu reviews the cases with the desk. They agree to ask every cash payout customer about an account, to post the day's rate at the counter, and to send Rahel Kassa a weekly list of beneficiaries with more than five transfers in a month.

takeaways: Remittances are small, frequent and cross-border, which attracts criminals; the AML/CFT law requires identification, records, monitoring and reporting.
FATF Recommendation 16 requires complete sender and beneficiary information with every wire transfer.
Structuring and money mules show up as patterns: many senders, amounts just under review levels, shared phone numbers, cash handed to someone waiting.
Screen before paying; clear only clear false positives and refer the rest.
Warn likely scam victims gently, record and refer; the desk escalates and compliance decides on a report.
Never tip off a customer about a report.

quiz.q: Which pattern most suggests structuring?
options: Eight transfers in ten days from six senders, each just under USD 1,000
One USD 300 transfer every month from a son
A quarterly USD 1,200 transfer by app
A single SWIFT transfer for school fees
quiz.explain: Many senders and amounts just below a review level are classic structuring signs.

quiz.q: Who decides whether to file a suspicious transaction report?
quiz.explain: The desk escalates; compliance decides and files with the Financial Intelligence Service.

quiz.q: What does FATF Recommendation 16 require?
options: Complete originator and beneficiary information with each wire transfer
quiz.explain: Recommendation 16 is the wire transfer rule on originator and beneficiary information.

quiz.q: A screening alert names a man born in 1961 of another nationality; the customer is an Ethiopian born in 1998. The officer should:
options: Clear it with a supervisor and record why, if the other details also differ
Refer to compliance and hold, whatever the details
quiz.explain: A clear false positive can be cleared on documented differences.

quiz.q: Telling a customer that a suspicious transaction report may be filed is called:
quiz.explain: Tipping off is forbidden by the AML/CFT law.

quiz.q: A family is asked by an online agent to send USD 800 to a personal account abroad for a Gulf job visa. This is most likely:
quiz.explain: Fees to a personal account through an unlicensed online agent are a classic job scam sign.

exam.q: Why does a formal remittance payout support Ethiopia's foreign exchange position, while an informal one does not?
options: Formal payouts are made in dollars
Formal payouts are exempt from tax
In a formal payout the foreign currency stays in the banking system, while a broker keeps it abroad
exam.explain: The family gets Birr either way, but only the formal channel adds the FX to the banking system.

exam.q: After FXD/01/2024, a broker offers Birr 154.00 per USD and the bank Birr 152.40. On USD 500, what does the broker pay extra, and is the deal lawful?
options: Birr 800; not lawful, FX may be dealt only through banks and authorized dealers
exam.explain: 500 x 1.60 = Birr 800, and Proclamation No. 1359/2025, Art. 39 limits FX dealing to banks and authorized dealers.

exam.q: A Gulf-corridor beneficiary normally receives USD 150 a month. Which change most deserves attention?
options: A transfer of USD 160 in one month
A transfer arriving two days late
Five transfers from five new senders in one week
A change from cash to wallet payout
exam.explain: A sudden pattern of new senders breaks the normal corridor profile and suggests structuring or mule activity.

exam.q: A SHA transfer of USD 3,000 has a USD 35 correspondent charge. Credited in Birr at Birr 152.40, what does the beneficiary receive?
A sender wants the beneficiary to receive the full amount of a SWIFT transfer. Which option should the sending bank use?
options: Any option, charges are never deducted
exam.explain: OUR makes the sender pay all charges.

exam.q: USD 520 is coming to a wallet that already holds Birr 0. At Birr 152.40, how does it compare with the reported ONPS/09/2023 balance limit?
exam.explain: 520 x 152.40 = Birr 79,248, which exceeds the Birr 75,000 balance limit; use an account credit.

exam.q: A bank's agent in a rural town has paid many transfers with handwritten ID numbers and no scans. What is the bank's position?
options: The MTO must investigate, not the bank
The bank is responsible for its agent and must review and act
No action is needed if no complaint was made
exam.explain: An agent acts for the bank, so the bank carries the compliance and fraud risk.

exam.q: Who must give the tracking number, sender name and expected amount at a payout?
options: The officer reads them to the customer
The customer gives them and the officer compares
exam.explain: Asking the customer first is the basic control against impostors.

exam.q: The ID shows "Mulugeta Abebbe" and the transfer says "Mulugeta Abebe"; all other details match. What is the right approach?
options: Ask the customer to change his ID
Follow the bank's procedure on spelling differences, with supervisor approval or a sender amendment as it requires
exam.explain: Transliteration differences are common; the bank's procedure says which a supervisor may accept.

exam.q: An elderly beneficiary has no ID and her grandson offers his Fayda ID. What should happen?
options: No payout until she can be identified; help her obtain an ID or ask the sender to change the beneficiary
Pay her on the grandson's guarantee
Cancel and refund in Birr at the desk
exam.explain: Only the named beneficiary, properly identified, may be paid; the desk cannot refund in Birr.

exam.q: USD 1,250 is paid out at Birr 152.40. If a 1% maximum charge applies to the payout amount, what is the highest charge?
A resident has already sent USD 1,800 for family support in the period. How much more may he send for that purpose under FXD/04/2026?
exam.explain: The limit is USD 3,000, so USD 3,000 - 1,800 = USD 1,200 remains.

exam.q: At a selling rate of Birr 155.50, a family support transfer of USD 2,800 costs how much Birr before tariff?
A diaspora customer's relative brings Birr from a local land sale to credit her USD diaspora account. The desk should:
options: Credit it once the customer signs a consent
Decline; diaspora FCY accounts must be funded from foreign sources
exam.explain: Local Birr cannot fund a diaspora FCY account under FXD/01/2024 as amended.

exam.q: A teller paid USD 600 at Birr 125.40 instead of Birr 152.40. What is the difference and how is it corrected?
options: Birr 16,200; pay from the till off the books
Birr 27,000; ask the MTO to resend
Birr 16,200; reverse and repost with maker and checker
exam.explain: 600 x 27 = Birr 16,200, corrected only by a controlled reversal and a correct entry.

exam.q: Which complaint answer best meets fair treatment duties?
options: "That is the rule, there is nothing to discuss"
"I have recorded your complaint under reference 214; the payout is held for an ID check, and you will hear from us by Thursday"
"We will refund your charges if you stop complaining"
exam.explain: Recording, explaining plainly and giving a time are the core of fair complaint handling.

exam.q: A student receives nine transfers totalling USD 8,560 from seven senders in 12 days. At Birr 152.40, what is the Birr total and the right step?
options: Birr 1,304,544; pay matching transfers and refer the pattern to compliance
Birr 1,304,544; refuse all and tell him he is reported
Birr 1,520,000; freeze his account at the desk
exam.explain: 8,560 x 152.40 = Birr 1,304,544. The desk escalates without tipping off; compliance decides on a report.

exam.q: Three different beneficiaries each hand their cash to the same man waiting at the branch door. This most likely indicates:
options: Money mules collecting for an organizer
exam.explain: Cash passed to the same third party is a classic mule pattern.

exam.q: A young customer says an online partner she has never met sent her USD 1,500 and asked her to forward most of it to three accounts. What should the desk do?
options: Pay on valid ID, warn her about the mule risk and refer to compliance
Tell her a report will be filed against her
exam.explain: The transfer can be paid, but she should be warned and the case referred, without tipping off.

exam.q: Which transfer should be queried before payout under the wire transfer rule?
options: An MTO transfer with matching tracking details
A SWIFT transfer with the ordering customer's name and address missing
A transfer from a son to his mother
exam.explain: FATF Recommendation 16 requires complete originator information with each transfer.
